newsitem.title: USA: Policymakers wind up quiet yet productive IMF meet.
newsitem.headline: Policymakers wind up quiet yet productive IMF meet.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
International economic policymakers on Thursday wound up one of their quietest, yet in some ways most productive, annual meetings in recent years.

With currency markets mostly calm and the world economy free of crises, policymakers at the International Monetary Fund/World Bank meeting were able to concentrate on helping the poor and preparing for the next world financial shock.

Big changes are looming in the world economy, with Europe's plans to launch a single currency in 1999 and the growing might of China, set to take control next July of financial dynamo Hong Kong, site of the 1997 annual meeting.

"The world economic situation is favourable," IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus told the final session of the 181-nation gathering. "The prospects for continued global economic expansion are good."
Economic growth is picking up throughout the world, including in sub-Sahara Africa, which until recently had seemed caught in a spiral of increasing poverty and despair.
To help ensure that the progress Africa has made continues, policymakers launched a new multibillion-dollar debt relief plan this week.

The initiative, which combines the forces of the World Bank, the IMF and the Paris Club of creditor countries, aims to lift the burden of debt-ridden poor nations that must spend the benefits of economic growth servicing their loans.
"This is a breakthrough," Bank President James Wolfensohn said. "It was very good news for the poor of the world."
But, he told policymakers in his closing speech Thurday, "The task is just now beginning. The task of implementation is before us."
Up to 20 countries, most of them in Africa, are expected to benefit from the plan, which could cost creditors as much as $7.7 billion.
Full details of the financing, including a controversial plan to sell IMF gold, have yet to be worked out.
However, the financing details have been worked out on another plan to double the emergency resources available to the IMF in times of crises, to about $50 billion.
The extra money will come from smaller industrial countries and up-and-coming emerging market economies such as South Korea, Singapore and Thailand.
The cooperation evident in putting together the so-called New Arrangements to Borrow mirrored a growing consensus among rich and poor about the best way ahead for the world economy.

"We do not anymore have the debate of the old times between populism and professional economics, but, rather, it is more and more recognised among policymakers that good economics is basically good politics," Israeli central bank Governor Jacob Frenkel said.

"That consensus," Rubin added, "is to open markets, not close them, free business to compete, not restrain them, reduce deficits, not sustain them, and invest publicly in people, infrastructure and other areas critical to future productivity."

With the world economy looking up and a consensus forming on the best way ahead, problems that have only been whispered about in past annual meetings, such as entrenched corruption in many countries, were discussed openly this year.
Wolfensohn led the charge against corruption, calling it a "cancer" and saying he had the backing of both creditor and borrower countries to attack it.

But all the harmony at the meeting does not mean that policy disputes are a thing of the past. This week's spat between Italy and France over Rome's potential membership in the planned European monetary union shows that even the new consensus can have cracks.

With the EMU looking increasingly likely to go ahead, policymakers are confronted with a host of questions about its impact on the world economy and the dollar's role at the centre of the international financial system.
The growing economic might of Asia in general and China in particular also threatens to change the constellation of a world economy long dominated by the West.
China, the world's fastest growing economy in recent years, seems to share the West's belief in the benefits to be gained from freeing up markets and welcoming foreign investment.
"At the end of the day, all of our countries are seeking similar goals, and each of our countries has a stake in all the others," Camdessus said.
